Note · Duarte — Resonate

4 min read867 wordsUpdated 2026-06-06notes/canon/canon-duarte-resonate.md

Canon · Cluster: Communication & Storytelling · Maps to Course 05 (Marketing & Brand), E7 (Exec Presence & Comms)

  • Source: Nancy Duarte, Resonate (2010)
  • Core claim: Presentations should follow story structure, not report structure. The presenter is not the hero — the audience is; the presenter is the mentor.
  • Framework:
  • The "what is" / "what could be" oscillation — alternate between the current reality and the proposed future; the gap creates tension that holds attention and pulls the audience forward.
  • End on "the new bliss" — the future state realized; leave them in the world you're proposing.
  • The audience is the hero (hero's-journey mapping) — they undergo the change; you guide.
  • Open with a strong "what is," build through repeated contrast, cross the threshold (the call to adventure / your ask), end at transformation.
  • Applies when: any persuasive presentation meant to move people to act or change — pitches, visions, launches, keynotes, change communications.
  • Breaks when: not every communication should be a story — a status update, a technical decision doc, or a data review is better served by Minto's answer-first pyramid (canon minto pyramid principle); story structure on routine info wastes everyone's time and reads as theatrical. The "what is/what could be" pattern is also formulaic when overused — audiences pattern-match the manipulation. And great structure can't rescue a weak underlying idea or false "bliss."
  • Practitioner counterpoint: (researched 2026-06-05 — r/PublicSpeaking corpus + Stanford GSB / TEDxEast transcripts) The durable technique people keep is Duarte's: contrast/tension (what is vs. what could be) is what holds a room — "you need to make this difference as big as possible… it works like a cliffhanger in a movie" (TEDxEast). But the corpus reveals where the book is silent: the loudest practitioner pain isn't structure, it's delivery under pressure. r/PublicSpeaking's top threads are dominated by it — "I want to be more articulate" (247↑), a vocal coach's "what most people get wrong about their speaking voice" (185↑), and a raw "Made a COMPLETE fool of myself at Toastmasters tonight" (117↑) describing "speaking as fast as an auctioneer, trembling hands… literally running away from the podium." A perfect "what is / what could be" spine dies if you can't hold the room while you deliver it. The emotional engine pairs with Sinek's "why" (canon sinek start with why) and Heath's "motivate the Elephant" (canon heath switch).
  • Researched layer (2026-06-05)
  • Canonical explanation (sourced): Duarte's whole method came from one drawn shape. After "two years of research" she sketched a presentation "figure," overlaid it on MLK's "I Have a Dream" and Steve Jobs's 2007 iPhone launch, and "it worked." The mechanism: "At the beginning of any presentation you need to show what you have… the status quo… and then compare that to what could be. You need to make this difference as big as possible… In the middle, one can move back and forth and oscillate between what is and what could be" — ending "with new hope… a new utopia" (TEDxEast). Crucially, the speaker is not the star: "the speaker is not the hero; the hero of our idea is the audience… You are not Luke Skywalker, you are Yoda."
  • Real application (mined): the Jobs teardown. Duarte maps the 90-minute iPhone keynote and shows him oscillating — "here's this new phone, and here are the competitors that suck" — then "he admires his own product… he models for the audience the emotions he wants them to feel," landing on the new bliss (the Gretzky "skate to where the puck is going" close). The companion Stanford GSB clip supplies the slide-level rule: every slide needs one big idea amplified by contrast, because the opposite of contrast is "camouflage… right now in slide decks, everything looks the same."
  • Where the corpus pushes back on the book: Resonate perfects structure but the r/PublicSpeaking corpus shows real audiences are won or lost on delivery and nerves, which the book barely touches — threads beg for help being "more articulate" (247↑) and confess freezing up, voice shaking, going "completely blank" in front of a group (195↑). A vocal coach's advice ("you probably speak too high when you're nervous," 185↑) does more for an average presenter on Monday than another oscillation will. Story structure is necessary, not sufficient.
  • Sources in corpus: TEDx Talks — "Nancy Duarte uncovers common structure of greatest communicators" (youtube.com/watch?v=1nYFpuc2Umk) · Stanford GSB — "Nancy Duarte: How to Create Better Visual Presentations" (youtube.com/watch?v=so9EJoQJc-0) · Stanford GSB — "Nancy Duarte: How to Tell a Story" (youtube.com/watch?v=9JrRQ1oQWQk) · r/PublicSpeaking "I want to be more articulate" (247↑), "I used to freeze up every time I spoke in front of people" (195↑), "I'm a vocal coach… what most people get wrong about their speaking voice" (185↑), "Made a COMPLETE fool of myself at Toastmasters tonight" (117↑).
  • Links: canon sinek start with why · canon minto pyramid principle · canon tufte visual display · canon heath switch

Rep

Take your next presentation. Rewrite the spine as alternating "what is" → "what could be" beats, ending on the new bliss. Make the audience the hero of the change, not you or your product.

Marks itself read when you reach the end.
